No particular details are available as to what key changes AMD would make on the display front for now, but each generation has brought new capabilities, so expect some updates on that front too.

AMD is expected to launch its RDNA 5 lineup sometime in 2027 , though everything will depend on the ease of memory supply and the normalization of the PC market.

There is fear that consumer graphics cards would be pushed further into 2028 , but to be honest, no one can confirm actual launch plans this early. With that said, AMD is seen gearing up support for its next-gen RDNA 5 lineup, which is a good sign that we will hear more from them soon enough.

item.title: NVIDIA’s Top-End B300 Servers Are Allegedly So Easy To Buy In China, It’s Only A “Matter Of Asking The Right Person” And Having $3 Million Available
item.description:
The U.S. export control list might have banned NVIDIA’s B300 AI chips from being shipped to China, but who would have thought that it could only take the right connections and a boatload of money to secure a set for yourself? That’s right, for the extremely affluent, the Blackwell Ultra hardware is within their grasp, with the latest report stating that these AI GPUs are reaching between $3 million and $3.4 million per eight-GPU system, resulting in a 5x to 6x markup over U.S. retail rates.

One Shenzhen-based consultant reportedly noted that opening an AI firm is as easy as heading to a different district and working out a deal with a broker

The latest set of details published by The Washington Post highlights the purchasing of NVIDIA’s top-tier AI accelerators as being one of the easiest tasks when living in China. After all, interested parties only have to walk into local electronics markets and speak with the right brokers, with the latest report stating that it’s “simply a matter of asking the right person.”

As for how these brokers get their hands on GPUs that are supposedly placed on a trade ban list, an on-the-ground visit to Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei electronics district revealed that a seller identified as “Wu” quoted approximately $3 million for an eight-GPU server outfitted with flagship B300 chips. Other local vendors dealing in Blackwell rack units listed comparable eight-GPU machines between $3 million and $3.4 million.

Previously, even if individuals living in China had immense levels of capital, the most that they could purchase was NVIDIA’s H200. Now, a Shenzhen-based consultant noted that if he ever wanted to launch an AI firm, he would simply head to Huaqiangbei and “work out a deal.”

As for how these B300 servers land in China, Wu states that his supply of restricted chips arrives through Hong Kong, though he claimed he didn’t know where the hardware originally comes from prior to reaching the territory. Another broker, Jason Cheng, revealed that China’s gray market pipeline has become so established that buyers from Russia and Iran fly directly to China to purchase restricted NVIDIA systems at steep markups rather than attempting to source them independently.

This gray market has also been stacking shipments of H200 chips, which were previously estimated to be listed for $900,000 for an 8-GPU server , translating into a 3x premium. The reason for these ludicrous prices is China’s escalating trade restrictions on NVIDIA’s AI hardware, making it exceptionally difficult for traders to get their hands on them, making these chips a prime entrant into China’s gray market.

Given that the country significantly lacks frontier AI model development without having thousands of B300 servers, it isn’t surprising to learn that clients are paying a 5x to 6x premium to obtain an edge in this brutally competitive space. Moreover, these sales point towards what could be the United States’ inefficiency in preventing export-restricted hardware from landing in China.

This isn’t the first time we’ve reported on a half-baked control system from the U.S., as NVIDIA’s H200 AI GPUs were reportedly found in ghost offices , which belonged to companies that had deep Chinese military connections. We also believe China Telecom had the right connections and deep pockets, because how else would the company have deployed 32 of NVIDIA’s B300 servers ?

If hardware already placed on the U.S. export control list can still find its way to China, what purpose do these restrictions serve? Enforcing a trade ban won’t work just through some paperwork, as there also needs to be thorough due diligence. After all, if the Chinese have become so dexterous in acquiring B300 chips, what’s stopping them from getting NVIDIA’s upcoming latest and greatest AI GPU, Vera Rubin ?

News Source: The Washington Post

item.title: Analyst Jeff Pu Says DRAM Prices Could Halve in 2028 as the AI Memory Boom Cools, but Cheaper RAM Isn’t Coming Next Year
item.description:
Jeff Pu has cut every quarter of his 2027 DRAM price forecast, and the note's first-ever 2028 scenario has prices halving in the base case, though he isn't calling the supercycle off.

GF Securities Is Still Constructive On Micron And SK Hynix Even After Cutting Every 2027 DRAM Quarter To Zero Growth

We have been tracking the memory crisis for a while now, and GF Securities' Jeff Pu has now cut every quarter of his 2027 DRAM contract price forecast in a post on X . Prices for 1Q to 4Q27 are seen at +6%, +3%, 0% and 0% QoQ, down from the prior +10%, +7%, +5% and +3%. For those unaware, contract prices are the rates memory makers and their big customers agree on for bulk shipments, and QoQ means compared with the quarter before, so DRAM prices keep climbing through the first half of 2027 and then stall in the second half, which is a notable shift for a market that has been priced for tightness all year.

According to a report by Zhitong Finance on the full GF note, two things are driving this. On the server side, GPU shortages have led Chinese cloud service providers, the datacenter operators known as hyperscalers, to trim server DRAM orders, which is around 1% of total DRAM demand and can be absorbed by US hyperscalers. The consumer side is weaker, with soft demand, spec downgrades and continued pressure on DDR4, which is why DDR4 players like Nanya and Winbond look far less rosy. On supply, GF still sees DRAM short of demand, with a sufficiency gap, meaning the shortfall between supply and demand, of -5%, -5% and -4% in 2026, 2027 and 2028, as HBM, the high-bandwidth memory that goes on AI chips, crowds out wafer capacity. Pu expects potential production cuts if weakness persists, which would help defend the floor of long-term agreements, the multi-year supply contracts signed with big buyers.

TrendForce had moved in the same direction a day earlier, cutting its 2027 DRAM revenue forecast to $1.15 trillion, still 69% YoY growth, and its NAND Flash forecast to $419.3 billion, which is 29% growth. The NAND side is the messier one, since Chinese hyperscalers began scaling back their 2027 enterprise SSD orders, the datacenter drives, in mid-4Q26 over GPU supply shortage concerns, and those cuts exceeded the additional orders placed by North American hyperscalers, while supply expands at the same time. On top of that, brands are expected to cut NAND capacity specs in PCs and phones to keep BOM, or bill of materials, costs in check. We have already seen consumer NAND prices decline by 20% , with another 5-10% drop expected in early 2027.

GF itself had cut its 2027 NAND price outlook on November 17, from +6%/+3%/0%/0% to flat in 1Q and declines through 4Q, citing weak mobile and PC demand plus Chinese cloud providers cutting enterprise SSD orders.

The more interesting part of the note is its first-ever 2028 scenario analysis. GF laid out three cases for conventional DRAM, a bear case at $4 per GB, a base case at $8 and a bull case at $12, which is -75%, -50% and -25% from 2027's $16 per GB, with the bear case labelled 'pre-AI pricing'. In plain terms, the middle case has DRAM prices halving in 2028, and the worst case takes them back to where they sat before the AI frenzy, while HBM is seen down 30%, 20% or flat depending on the case.

Interestingly, Pu had already turned positive on DRAM back in September after prior bearish notes in July, so this revision is more of a moderation than a turnaround.

For now, none of this points to cheaper RAM arriving anytime soon. DRAM contract prices are still going up in 2027, just at a slower pace, and the supply side hasn't loosened either, since we have reported that SK hynix expects shortages to persist through 2030 despite expansion, with 50% of capacity going towards long-term agreements through 2027-2028. The relief is showing up on the SSD side instead, and NAND prices are expected to keep sliding into early 2027.

item.title: HPE CEO Antonio Neri Says AI Cloud Companies Are “Not A Use Of Our Capital” And Sales To Them Require “Guarantees And Prepayments”
item.description:
HPE CEO Antonio Neri believes that investing in neoclouds is not a good use of his firm's capital. Neoclouds are data center infrastructure providers that cater primarily to the needs of the artificial intelligence industry. Neri made the remarks while talking to Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, and his thoughts echo those of others, including Elon Musk, who have raised concerns about neocloud sustainability.

HPE CEO Says Firm Is Focused On Enterprise & Sovereign Computing & Not Neoclouds

The booming demand for AI GPUs, primarily from NVIDIA, comes even as their prices remain high and the memory chip industry continues to experience shortages. Consequently, neoclouds, including infrastructure giant CoreWeave, have to rely on costly debt to finance their purchases with the belief that demand from AI companies and the subsequent monetization will make their spending worth it.

However, HPE CEO Antonio Neri believes that the neocloud business is not an efficient use of his firm's capital. When asked by Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi why HPE was not investing in neoclouds, Neri remarked:

"We believe that's not a use of our capital. You know, we finance obviously very high credit quality customers. All of them are in the enterprise space."

Neri added that instead of necolouds, HP was investing in enterprise computing and sovereign AI instead. Sovereign AI refers to infrastructure set up by nation-states to meet their AI needs. The HPE CEO believes that these two segments are "where we believe the growth will be down the road. So we are establishing ourselves a footprint."

As to why his firm is investing in enterprise, he added:

"We know how to manage the assets in enterprise. The return on equity in that business today was 25%. And the loss ratio of the book of business we have with an amazing set of assets is 0.3%."

However, not investing in neoclouds doesn't mean HP doesn't do business with them. As a server equipment manufacturer, the firm sells equipment to them. But the sales follow a process, as Neri outlined:

"And so we believe that's not how we want to use the capital. We do business with neoclouds but of course we work with commercial terms that requires you know all sorts of guarantees and prepayments."

The HPE CEO isn't the only one who's critical of neoclouds. Late last month, Elon Musk discussed neoclouds and simply predicted that "200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation." The reason behind the pessimism was financing, as Musk outlined that "debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers."
